The HTTP/3 Protocol
The HTTP/3 Protocol element represents a Protocol Handler component that supports the HTTP/3 protocol (RFC 9114) over the QUIC transport (RFC 9000).
Unlike HTTP/2, HTTP/3 is not an upgrade of an existing protocol: it runs directly over UDP and always uses TLS 1.3 (RFC 9001). An HTTP/3 connector is therefore configured as a standalone connector by setting its protocol attribute to one of the HTTP/3 protocol classes and its SSLEnabled attribute to true. The protocol class also selects the QUIC transport implementation: org.apache.coyote.http3.Http3OpenSSLProtocol uses the OpenSSL QUIC endpoint, org.apache.coyote.http3.Http3QuicheProtocol uses the Cloudflare quiche endpoint, and org.apache.coyote.http3.Http3Ngtcp2Protocol uses the ngtcp2 transport. Certificates are configured through nested SSLHostConfig and Certificate elements, as described in the HTTP Connector document. The OpenSSL QUIC endpoint accepts PEM files (with the key and certificate chain supplied separately), PKCS#12 files and Java keystores; the quiche endpoint currently loads its certificate from PEM files.
HTTP/3 support requires the FFM bindings to be compiled into the build (a current JDK) plus a usable QUIC transport: for Http3OpenSSLProtocol, an OpenSSL installation that provides the QUIC API (OpenSSL 4.0 or later) loaded into the JVM via the FFM bindings - see the OpenSSLLifecycleListener configuration in the default conf/server.xml; for Http3QuicheProtocol, a loadable libquiche; for Http3Ngtcp2Protocol, a system libngtcp2 from the 1.16.x or 1.26.x series plus libngtcp2_crypto_ossl backed by the system OpenSSL 3.5 or later (ngtcp2 uses a normal TLS server context rather than the OpenSSL QUIC API). The connector fails at bind time when the selected transport is unusable. The sample conf/server.xml also configures a TLS connector on the TCP side of the same port with altService="h3" so that HTTP/3 is discovered by clients through the Alt-Svc response header.
The HTTP/3 protocol handler supports the following attributes on the connector:
The alternative service which should be advertised as available to clients via the Alt-Svc response header. The value is a protocol identifier, for example h3, and must be a valid HTTP token (RFC 9110 Section 5.6.2); the port advertised is the port of the request the header is added to. An Alt-Svc header set by the application takes precedence. A null or empty value disables the header. If not specified, no Alt-Svc header is added.
A boolean value which can be used to enable or disable the consistency check for the scheme presented by the user agent in the :scheme pseudo-header and the channel over which the request was received. Since QUIC always uses TLS, the consistent scheme is https. This should only be set to true where a trusted TLS terminating reverse proxy is used. If not specified, this attribute is set to false.
The value is a comma separated list of MIME types for which HTTP compression may be used. The default value is
text/html,text/xml,text/plain,text/css,text/javascript,application/javascript,application/json,application/xml . If you specify a type explicitly, the default is over-ridden.
The Connector may use GZIP compression in an attempt to save server bandwidth. The acceptable values for the parameter is "off" (disable compression), "on" (allow compression, which causes text data to be compressed), "force" (forces compression in all cases), or a numerical integer value (which is equivalent to "on", but specifies the minimum amount of data before the output is compressed). If the content-length is not known and compression is set to "on" or more aggressive, the output will also be compressed. If not specified, this attribute is set to "off".
Note that HTTP/3 forbids the Transfer-Encoding header (RFC 9114 Section 4.2). A request whose TE header carries any value other than trailers — including one that asks for compression through TE rather than through Accept-Encoding — is rejected as a malformed field section.
If compression is set to "on" then this attribute may be used to specify the minimum amount of data before the output is compressed. If not specified, this attribute is defaults to "2048". Units are in bytes.
A comma-separated list of the :protocol values this connector supports for an Extended CONNECT request (RFC 9220 Section 3). Matching is case-insensitive (RFC 9110 Section 7.8) and whitespace around each value is ignored. When enableConnectProtocol is enabled, an Extended CONNECT carrying a :protocol value that is not listed is answered with 501 by the connector rather than being dispatched to the application; with the default empty list, every Extended CONNECT is answered with 501. When enableConnectProtocol is disabled (the default), the peer has not been told that Extended CONNECT is permitted (RFC 9220 Section 3.2), so a request carrying :protocol is rejected earlier by request validation as a malformed message (a stream error of type H3_MESSAGE_ERROR) and the 501 path is not reached. The configured values are local policy and are not advertised in the HTTP/3 SETTINGS frame; only enableConnectProtocol controls the SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL advertisement.
When to respond with a 100 intermediate response code to a request containing an Expect: 100-continue header. The following values may be used:
immediately (the default) - an intermediate 100 status response will be returned as soon as practical
onRead - an intermediate 100 status response will be returned only when the Servlet reads the request body, allowing the servlet to inspect the headers and possibly respond before the user agent sends a possibly large request body.
A boolean value which controls whether Extended CONNECT (RFC 9220) is permitted. When enabled, the value 1 is advertised to peers via SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL and requests carrying a :protocol pseudo-header are accepted, subject to the connectProtocols list. An Extended CONNECT whose :protocol value is not registered in that list is answered with 501 by the connector. Plain CONNECT and supported Extended CONNECT requests are passed to the application; the current Servlet container implementation then intercepts every CONNECT request (plain or Extended) with a 501 response before the application, so enabling this attribute does not currently make an application-visible CONNECT tunnel available. RFC 9220 tunnels carry application data in ordinary HTTP/3 DATA frames; HTTP datagrams (RFC 9297) are a separate extension used by WebTransport and are not required for a CONNECT tunnel. If not specified, this attribute is set to false.
A boolean value which controls whether Tomcat advertises the experimental, unregistered H2_COMPATIBLE_IDENTITY setting (identifier 0x22). Peers that do not recognise the setting ignore it. If not specified, this attribute is set to false.
The QUIC connection idle timeout in milliseconds (RFC 9000 Section 10.1). If no packet is received from the peer for this duration the connection is closed. The value is also advertised to the peer in the TLS transport parameters so that both endpoints agree on the timeout. The OpenSSL endpoint can reject the feature request if the first TLS flight has already been generated, in which case the OpenSSL default applies and a warning is logged. Zero or a negative value leaves the transport default in place. Values above 9223372036854 (the largest millisecond value whose conversion to microseconds does not overflow a Java long) are rejected with an IllegalArgumentException. If not specified, a default of 30000 (30 seconds) is used.
The maximum number of active request streams permitted for any one connection. The value must be greater than zero and no greater than 2^60 (the largest valid QUIC stream count, RFC 9000 Sections 4.6 and 18.2); values outside this range are rejected with an IllegalArgumentException. If a client attempts to open more active streams than this limit, the additional streams are refused. The effective limit is clamped to the limit the QUIC transport actually advertises to the peer. If not specified, a default of 100 is used.
The maximum field section size, in bytes, that this endpoint is willing to decode (RFC 9114 Section 4.2.2). The value is enforced on incoming field sections and advertised to peers via SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE. A value of 0 is enforced as an explicit zero-byte local limit and is advertised as 0, so peers do not apply the RFC 9114 default of unlimited. A negative value is treated locally as 0 and is likewise advertised as 0. Positive values above 4473915 (the largest decoded field section that fits the 16 MiB per-frame buffer after the QPACK wire overhead) are clamped to that effective limit for the local decoder, the advertisement and the inbound frame preflight. If not specified, a default of 16384 is used.
The limit is a decoded field-section size. The receiver's frame preflight and pending-payload buffer retain the corresponding wire bytes, bounded by Constants.fieldSectionWireLimit(limit) (approximately 15/4 times the decoded limit plus 32 bytes, and in practice by the 16 MiB per-frame limit). Each stream can therefore retain up to that wire-side bound while its field section is being assembled; the worst-case per-connection buffering is the wire-side bound per stream multiplied by maxConcurrentStreams (plus any trailer sections when maxTrailerSize is negative, also capped at 16 MiB per stream). The default limits are deliberately small; raising this value to the effective maximum should account for the configured concurrency using the wire-side bound, not the decoded limit.
In addition to the retained wire bytes, each Huffman-coded string literal is decoded before the decoded field-section limit is applied. The shortest RFC 7541 Huffman code is five bits, so the decoded character buffer can temporarily be up to 8/5 times the encoded length (about 1.6 times the wire bound, and about six times the configured decoded limit in the worst case). This transient buffer is released after the literal is decoded, but memory sizing for a raised limit should include it per concurrently decoded stream. The same transient expansion applies while decoding QPACK encoder-stream insertions, bounded by the advertised dynamic-table capacity rather than by maxFieldSectionSize.
A comma-separated list of content encodings that indicate already-compressed content. When the response already has a Content-Encoding header with one of these values, compression will not be applied to prevent double compression. This attribute is only used if compression is set to on or force.
If not specified, the default value is br,compress,dcb,dcz,deflate,gzip,pack200-gzip,zstd, which includes all commonly used compression algorithms.
The value is a regular expression (using java.util.regex) matching the entire user-agent header of HTTP clients for which compression should not be used, because these clients, although they do advertise support for the feature, have a broken implementation. The default value is an empty String (regexp matching disabled).
The maximum number of request streams per connection that may block waiting for dynamic table entries announced on the peer's QPACK encoder stream (RFC 9204 Section 2.1.2). The value must be zero or greater; a negative value is rejected with an IllegalArgumentException. A positive value is advertised to peers via SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS. A value of 0 disables stream blocking: field sections that reference entries not yet present in the dynamic table are then treated as a decompression failure. If not specified, a default of 0 is used.
Each blocked request can wait up to qpackBlockedStreamTimeoutMs for an insert that never arrives. With a positive value and a large maxThreads or maxConcurrentStreams configuration, a peer can occupy many container request threads for that duration. The default of 0 avoids this; increase the value only for clients known to use the dynamic table and keep it small relative to the thread pool.
The maximum time in milliseconds a request stream may block waiting for an insert on the peer's QPACK encoder stream (RFC 9204 Section 2.1.2) when qpackBlockedStreams is positive. The value must be greater than zero and at most 9223372036854 (the largest millisecond value whose conversion to nanoseconds does not overflow a Java long); out-of-range values are rejected with an IllegalArgumentException. A blocked stream pins one container worker thread for up to this duration. If not specified, a default of 5000 (five seconds) is used.
The maximum QPACK dynamic table capacity in bytes. The value must be between 0 and 4194304 (4 MiB); values outside this range are rejected with an IllegalArgumentException. The value is advertised to peers via SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY and the local decoder is sized to match, as required for interoperability (RFC 9204 Section 5). A value of 0 disables the dynamic table entirely. If not specified, a default of 4096 is used.
The dynamic table is per connection. Its ring array, entry objects and retained name/value strings all scale with this capacity, so the decoder can use several times the configured value in memory for each connection. The 4 MiB hard limit bounds that amplification; raising the value should account for the number of concurrent connections. Encoder instructions are decoded into temporary strings before the entry-size check rejects an oversized entry, so a large capacity also allows a correspondingly larger transient allocation while instruction bytes are being processed.
QPACK encoder-stream instructions are processed on the QUIC poll thread for the connection. A peer that continuously churns the table, or a large request field section being decoded on a worker thread while the poll thread waits for the shared decoder lock, can delay other connection events. The default capacity is small; raising it increases both the memory and the possible processing time per instruction.
QPACK encoder-stream instructions are re-assembled in the per-stream read buffer. If this capacity is increased significantly, increase readBufferSize as well: a legal Huffman-encoded insert may be up to approximately 15/4 of the table capacity in wire bytes, and an instruction that cannot fit in the read buffer is rejected with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD.
The value used for the Server header in any HTTP/3 response created by this connector. If configured, it always overrides any value the application may have set. If not specified, no Server header is set by the connector; an application-provided value stands unless serverRemoveAppProvidedValues is enabled.
If set to true, any Server header provided by the application is removed from HTTP/3 responses when no server value is configured. If not specified, this attribute is set to false.
The following connector attributes are handled by the QUIC endpoint that backs the HTTP/3 protocol handler:
The maximum number of concurrent QUIC connections the endpoint accepts. Connections opened above this limit are refused. If not specified, a default of 8192 is used.
The timeout, in milliseconds, used for each iteration of the endpoint's QUIC poll loop. Smaller values reduce event latency at the cost of more frequent wake-ups. Values outside the range 1 to 60000 are rejected with a warning and the previous value is retained. If not specified, a default of 10 is used.
The size, in bytes, of the per-stream read buffer maintained by the endpoint. Values below 1 are rejected with a warning and the previous value is retained. Stream data is drained in chunks of at most 65536 bytes by the quiche endpoint, whose native read buffer is capped at the maximum datagram size; the OpenSSL endpoint reads up to the buffer's remaining capacity in a single call. Either way, larger values are filled by repeated reads. Control-stream frames and QPACK encoder-stream instructions are re-assembled in this buffer; a value substantially below the largest SETTINGS frame or QPACK instruction the deployment must accept causes conformant peers to be rejected with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD rather than merely slowed down. If not specified, a default of 16384 is used.
Upper bound, in milliseconds, of the adaptive floor the OpenSSL QUIC endpoint's poll loop applies to due-deadline (timer) ticks: while such ticks fire back-to-back without any reactive work, the floor doubles from 20 ms up to this value, coalescing the ticks; it resets as soon as the loop performs reactive work. A value of 0 disables the floor, running every tick the engine reports as due. Values outside the range 0 to 60000 are rejected with a warning and the previous value is retained. If not specified, a default of 50 is used. The quiche endpoint has no due-tick floor and does not support this attribute.
The HTTP/3 connector also supports the following attributes, which are documented in the HTTP Connector document:
allowedTrailerHeaders
maxHeaderCount
maxThreads
maxTrailerCount
maxTrailerSize
relaxedPathChars
relaxedQueryChars
For HTTP/3, a negative maxTrailerSize disables the decoded trailer-size limit, but the receiver still enforces the 16 MiB per-frame buffering limit. As with maxFieldSectionSize, trailer payload is retained per request stream, so the per-connection worst case scales with maxConcurrentStreams.
A DATA or HEADERS frame on a request stream whose declared payload exceeds 16 MiB is rejected at the frame header with RESET_STREAM and error code H3_FRAME_ERROR. The frame is protocol-valid (HTTP/3 has no negotiated frame-size limit), so this is a local implementation limit; for DATA it applies even though the payload could otherwise be streamed.
For HTTP/3, allowedTrailerHeaders filters the incoming request trailer fields that are exposed to the application, just as it does for chunked HTTP/1.1 input. It has no effect on outgoing response trailer fields; those are filtered by a separate fixed list of field names that cannot appear in trailers (for example Content-Length, Host and TE). The allow-list cannot override that fixed list for incoming trailers either: a field that is prohibited in trailers by RFC 9110 Section 6.5.1 is ignored even when it is explicitly allowed.
Note that send file support is not available over QUIC: response bodies are always written through the output buffer as HTTP/3 DATA frames.
At TRACE level the HTTP/3 implementation logs encoded and decoded header names and values, which may include authorization tokens, cookies and other credentials. At DEBUG level, exception messages for malformed headers can include field names, field values, Host values and SNI names; control bytes are rendered as 0xNN, but other peer-controlled text remains visible. Treat both TRACE and DEBUG logs as potentially sensitive and restrict access to them.
In addition to the configurable limits above, the HTTP/3 implementation applies the following fixed per-connection or per-request limits to bound memory and processing. Exceeding a limit is reported to the peer with the error code shown. These values are implementation constants; they are not configurable connector attributes.
A SETTINGS frame may carry at most 4096 setting identifiers; exceeding the limit fails the connection with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD.
Inbound QPACK instructions on the encoder and decoder streams combined are limited to 262144 instructions and 128 MiB of instruction bytes per connection; exceeding either budget fails the connection with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD.
At most 65536 QPACK decoder instructions (Section Acknowledgment, Stream Cancellation and Insert Count Increment) may be pending per connection; exceeding the pending-instruction limit fails the connection with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD.
The buffer of pre-open PRIORITY_UPDATE signals holds at most min(4096, max(16, maxConcurrentStreams)) entries (the ceiling is 4096; the concurrent-stream limit lowers it, with a floor of 16 when that limit is smaller than 16); the oldest least-recently-used entries are evicted. This is a memory bound and does not fail the connection.
Known client control-stream frames are limited to 65536 frames and 32 MiB of declared payload per connection; exceeding either budget fails the connection with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD.
Unknown control-stream frames are limited to 16384 frames and 64 MiB of declared payload per connection; data discarded from unknown unidirectional streams is limited to 64 MiB per connection. Exceeding either budget fails the connection with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD.
Padding and other non-body frames on request streams are limited to 16384 frames and 64 MiB per request, and to 262144 frames and 256 MiB for the lifetime of a connection; exceeding either budget fails the connection with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD.
A DATA or HEADERS frame whose declared payload exceeds 16 MiB is rejected with RESET_STREAM and H3_FRAME_ERROR (see above).
At most 64 KiB of request body is buffered before dispatch. The pre-dispatch body buffer is allocated lazily, and grows only as DATA payload actually arrives, so a peer-declared Content-Length (or DATA frame length) cannot force the full allocation before any body byte is received. The remainder is read on demand and does not fail the request.
A blocking request-body read waits at most the configured read timeout, or 30 seconds when none is configured, before the stream is reset with H3_REQUEST_INCOMPLETE or H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED and the read fails with a timeout.
The QPACK dynamic table capacity is capped at 4 MiB (see qpackMaxTableCapacity).
The ordered non-blocking response write queue is bounded to 256 KiB of queued frames after the current application write. One application write larger than that bound is accepted as a single oversized batch at the head of an otherwise empty queue; frames from later writes are counted against the bound. If the bound is exceeded, the frame is dropped and the response stream is reset with H3_INTERNAL_ERROR.
An HTTP/3 connector requires at least one nested SSLHostConfig element since QUIC mandates TLS 1.3. Each SSLHostConfig needs at least one Certificate or PreSharedKey element. These elements are the same as those used by the HTTP Connector.
TLS 1.3 external pre-shared keys are supported by the OpenSSL QUIC and ngtcp2 endpoints; the quiche endpoint does not support them. A connection that offers a configured identity is authenticated with the pre-shared key and the server presents no certificate. An SSLHostConfig that has both certificates and pre-shared keys serves both: connections with a resolvable identity get a pre-shared key handshake, connections with an unknown identity or with no identity at all get the normal certificate handshake. An SSLHostConfig configured with pre-shared keys only presents no certificate; a connection that does not offer a usable identity then fails the handshake.
Client certificates (mutual TLS) are not supported: the certificateVerification attribute of SSLHostConfig is ignored by all QUIC endpoints and no client certificate is ever requested during the TLS handshake. The quiche endpoint logs a warning at start-up when the attribute is configured with a value other than none.
TLS session resumption is supported by all QUIC endpoints through TLS 1.3 session tickets: the server issues a ticket after each handshake and a client offering a ticket from an earlier connection to the same endpoint completes the handshake without a full key exchange. The ticket keys are generated randomly when the endpoint starts, so a ticket is only valid for the running endpoint instance that issued it: after a restart (and, for the quiche endpoint, after a certificate reload, which rebuilds the TLS configuration) older tickets can no longer be decrypted and a client offering one simply performs a full handshake. Ticket keys are not configurable, so tickets do not span separate Tomcat instances. The OpenSSL QUIC endpoint honours the disableSessionTickets attribute of SSLHostConfig; the quiche endpoint has no equivalent switch and always issues tickets.
HTTP/3 connections are discovered by clients through the Alt-Svc response header. The usual arrangement is a TLS connector on the TCP side of the same port with altService="h3" announcing the HTTP/3 endpoint, as shown in the default conf/server.xml. An HTTP/3 connector does not announce itself automatically; set its altService attribute when an announcement from the HTTP/3 side is wanted.
Response compression is supported for HTTP/3. The connector applies the same compression, compressionMinSize, compressibleMimeType, noCompressionEncodings and noCompressionUserAgents configuration as the HTTP/1.1 connector. When compression is used, the response body is GZIP encoded and carried in HTTP/3 DATA frames; the content coding is applied by the connector, not by the application.
